T1: Musicians will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it does not impede listening and performing, because they currently avoid standard earplugs due to sound distortion. Who benefits: Musicians who need to hear their performances and audience clearly.. Why behaviour changes: If a product reduces sound distortion while still providing adequate protection, musicians will switch from avoiding earplugs to actively using them.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for models that preserve sound quality, and can sell directly to musicians via online channels.. Assumptions: Musicians are willing to pay more for a product that does not compromise sound quality.; There is sufficient awareness of Hellberg among musicians to reach them directly.; The product can be produced at a price point that justifies a premium.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard vs. sound-preserving), musicians will choose the sound-preserving version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Purchase intent will be higher among musicians who report sound distortion as a barrier to using earplugs..

T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is lightweight, comfortable, and seamlessly integrates with outdoor gear, because they currently avoid earplugs due to bulk and lack of compatibility with activities. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who need protection without compromising mobility or gear integration.. Why behaviour changes: If a product is designed for outdoor use (e.g., waterproof, lightweight, compatible with helmets/headlamps), users will switch from not using earplugs to actively wearing them during activities.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price a premium outdoor-specific model and sell through outdoor retailers and direct-to-consumer channels, capturing value through volume sales and brand extension.. Assumptions: Outdoor enthusiasts are willing to pay more for a product that does not restrict movement or compatibility.; There is sufficient market awareness of Hellberg among outdoor users to reach them.; The product can be produced at a price point that justifies a premium for outdoor features.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard vs. outdoor-specific), outdoor enthusiasts will choose the outdoor-specific version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Purchase intent will be higher among outdoor enthusiasts who report bulk/compatibility as a barrier to using earplugs..

Test "Musician vs Outdoor Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 respondents: 100 self-identified musicians (recruited via music forums and social media) and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and social media).. Measure: 1) Choice: respondents view two versions of a Hellberg earplug prototype: Standard (no sound preservation) and Sound-Preserving (uses proprietary technology to reduce distortion while maintaining protection). They select which version they would buy. 2) WTP: respondents state the maximum price they would pay for each version (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Musicians will choose the Sound-Preserving version at a rate ≥55% and will report a WTP ≥ €30 for it, indicating they value sound preservation over standard protection.; T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will choose the Sound-Preserving version at a rate <40% and will report a WTP < €25 for it, indicating they prioritize comfort/bulk over sound preservation.. Decision rule: If the observed choice rate for the Sound-Preserving version among musicians is ≥55% AND the average WTP for musicians is ≥ €30, proceed with developing a differentiated musician proposition. If the observed choice rate for the Sound-Preserving version among outdoor enthusiasts is <40% AND the average WTP for outdoor enthusiasts is < €25, proceed with developing a differentiated outdoor proposition. If neither. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether musicians would adopt a sound-preserving version and whether outdoor enthusiasts would adopt an outdoor-specific version. The test will determine whether there is sufficient demand and willingness to pay for each segment before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This does not address whether musicians would switch to a sound-preserving version, nor does it quantify willingness to pay. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether musicians would adopt a sound-preserving version and whether outdoor enthusiasts would adopt an outdoor-specific version. The test will determine whether there is sufficient demand and willingness to pay for each segment before committing resources. Target customer: Musicians (for sound-preserving proposition) and outdoor enthusiasts (for outdoor-specific proposition). Value proposition: A differentiated Hellberg earplug that either preserves sound quality for musicians or integrates seamlessly with outdoor gear for enthusiasts, positioned as a premium product with willingness to pay tested before launch.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute Test X1 within the €12,000 budget and 10‑week timeline, recruiting 200 respondents (100 musicians and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) and measuring choice and willingness-to-pay for the sound-preserving version.. Uncertainty: Demand for a sound-preserving version among musicians and willingness to pay €30+; demand for an outdoor-specific version among outdoor enthusiasts and willingness to pay €25+; overall market size and competitive landscape for each segment.. Would change if: If the choice rate for the sound-preserving version among musicians is ≥55% and the average willingness-to-pay is ≥€30, proceed with developing a musician-focused proposition.; If the choice rate for the outdoor-specific version among outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and the average willingness-to-pay is ≥€25, proceed with developing an outdoor-focused proposition.; If neither segment meets its respective thresholds, reconsider expansion or license the technology to third‑party brands.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Recruit 200 participants: 100 self-identified musicians and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers). Each participant views a product description of a high-fidelity earplug (for musicians) or a lightweight outdoor earplug (for outdoor users). They are asked: "Would you purchase this product?" (binary) and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open-ended).. Sample: 200 participants (100 musicians, 100 outdoor users). Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Musicians will show purchase intent ≥30% and willingness to pay ≥1.5x standard earplugs.; T2: Outdoor users will show purchase intent ≥25% and willingness to pay ≥1.2x standard earplugs.. Decision rule: If musicians’ purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness to pay ≥ 1.5x standard earplugs, proceed with musician-focused proposition. If outdoor users’ purchase intent ≥ 25% and willingness to pay ≥ 1.2x standard earplugs, proceed with outdoor-focused proposition. If neither met. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed test (Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test) to empirically validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed test (Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test) to empirically validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Musicians and outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers) who currently avoid standard earplugs due to sound quality or bulk.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protection product that either maintains sound fidelity for musicians or is lightweight and comfortable for outdoor users, sold through existing B2B channels and new consumer channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test (200 participants, 100 musicians, 100 outdoor users, €15,000, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for each segment.. Uncertainty: Demand for a high-fidelity musician product is uncertain due to lack of direct evidence; outdoor demand is also uncertain due to lack of market data.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Creators who use equipment to build a personal brand and attract clients.. Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) a premium, branded home body-fat analyser marketed for personal health monitoring; (B) a niche-branded home body-fat analyser marketed for athletes and fitness enthusiasts. Both descriptions include price points (e.g., €250 for premium, €150 for niche) and a brief product description. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale and. Sample: 500 adults aged 25‑55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region (Japan, US, Europe).. Measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) for each product description.. Predictions: T1: Premium product will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the niche product (difference ≥ 1.5 points).; T2: Niche product will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the premium product (difference ≥ 1.5 points).. Decision rule: If premium product mean ≥ niche product mean + 1.5 points, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If niche product mean ≥ premium product mean + 1.5 points, proceed with niche athlete proposition. If difference < 1.5 points, inconclusive; consider. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on B2B markets and existing product lines. Conduct a targeted survey test (as proposed) to empirically compare purchase intent for a premium, branded home body-fat analyser versus a niche-branded athlete version before any larger investment. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Musicians will adopt hearing protection if it does not impede sound quality, because they rely on hearing the music accurately for performance and enjoyment. Who benefits: Musicians and early‑career musicians who perform regularly and need reliable hearing protection without compromising auditory performance.. Why behaviour changes: The identified barrier of the impact of HPDs on listening to music and performing (couth-2022-musicians) makes musicians reluctant to use HPDs. If a product is marketed as not affecting sound quality, they will be more willing to adopt it.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for models designed for musicians, sell directly to consumers via online channels, and build brand reputation as the preferred hearing protection for musicians.. Assumptions: Musicians value sound fidelity as much as safety.; A segment of musicians is willing to pay more for a product that does not compromise sound.; Hellberg can design a product that meets both safety and sound-quality standards.. Predictions: If offered a musician‑focused product with clear sound‑fidelity claims, at least 20% of surveyed musicians will express intent to purchase within 4 weeks.; Sales of a musician‑focused line will be positively correlated with the proportion of musicians who report sound‑quality concerns as a barrier..

T2: Industrial workers will adopt hearing protection if it is integrated into existing safety gear and does not require additional training or disruption to workflow, because they already follow safety protocols and need compatible equipment. Who benefits: Industrial employers and safety managers who need to comply with regulations and reduce injury rates, and workers who prefer seamless integration of PPE.. Why behaviour changes: Workers currently avoid hearing protection due to perceived inconvenience, lack of time for training, and the need for equipment that does not interfere with tasks. A product that fits existing safety gear and requires no additional steps. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell through industrial distributors, offer bundled safety kits, and charge a premium for integrated solutions, capturing value through volume sales and reduced support costs.. Assumptions: Industrial safety managers prioritize compliance and cost-effectiveness.; Workers will adopt PPE if it does not disrupt workflow.; Hellberg can design a product that meets industrial safety standards without major modifications.. Predictions: If offered an integrated hearing protection solution to industrial buyers, at least 15% of surveyed buyers will express intent to purchase within 6 weeks.; Purchase intent will be positively correlated with the proportion of buyers who report current PPE adoption rates above 70%..

Test "Musician vs Industrial Buyer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Recruit 200 participants: 100 self-identified musicians (aged 18-45) and 100 industrial workers (aged 25-55) with safety responsibility. Randomly assign each participant to one of two product variations: (A) Musician-focused product claiming no impact on sound quality; (B) Integrated industrial product claiming seamless workflow integration. Participants view product descriptions, price €120, and are asked: "If the product met your needs, would you be likely to purchase within 4 weeks?" (Likert 1-5).. Sample: 200 participants (100 musicians, 100 industrial workers). Measure: Purchase intent score (1-5) for each product variant within each segment.. Predictions: T1: Musician segment: mean intent for musician-focused product >=3.5; industrial segment: mean intent for musician-focused product <2.5; T2: Industrial segment: mean intent for integrated industrial product >=3.5; musician segment: mean intent for integrated industrial product <2.5. Decision rule: If musician-focused mean intent >=3.5 and integrated industrial mean intent <2.5, proceed with musician-focused proposition. If integrated industrial mean intent >=3.5 and musician mean intent <2.5, proceed with integrated industrial proposition. If both. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.; Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.; Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.. Predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.; Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.. How value is captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.. Assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.; Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.; Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.; Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, multi‑purpose model (one compact tractor performing multiple tasks) and a status‑oriented model (same tractor styled with modern aesthetic, premium pricing). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary).. Sample: 500 U.S. households with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.. Measure: 1) WTP: maximum price participants would pay for each tractor concept. 2) Purchase intent: percentage indicating "Very likely" to buy each concept. 3) Secondary: perceived practicality (1‑10 scale) and perceived status (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Functional tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than status tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 10%.; T2: Status tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than functional tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 15%.. Decision rule: If functional tractor meets both WTP and purchase intent thresholds (e.g., purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ $2,500) and status tractor does not meet either threshold, proceed with a differentiated functional consumer proposition. If status tractor meets both thresholds and functional tractor does not, proceed with a differentiated status‑oriented consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds, . Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to empirically test whether a functional, multi‑purpose tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. If the survey confirms the functional model, proceed to develop a differentiated functional consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to empirically test whether a functional, multi‑purpose tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. If the survey confirms the functional model, proceed to develop a differentiated functional consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion. Target customer: Small‑holder households with limited storage space and budget, who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Value proposition: A compact, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor that performs several tasks without compromising durability, sold at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, leveraging Deere’s engineering and existing dealer network.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Preference Survey (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €15,000 budget.. Uncertainty: Both T1 (functional demand) and T2 (status demand) remain uncertain due to limited public evidence of consumer motivations in the 1960s.. Would change if: If the survey shows the status‑oriented tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds, shift focus to a differentiated status‑oriented proposition.; If neither tractor meets thresholds, abandon consumer expansion or pursue a different route to market.. Why behaviour changes: Legal requirement for registration and mandatory use in remote environments creates a compliance-driven demand; users trust devices that have proven track record of saving lives.. Test "Consumer vs Government Demand Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and clubs) and (B) Emergency services/outdoor organizations (recruited via SAR agency and park management contacts). Both groups view a product description of the 406 MHz PLB highlighting compliance, reliability, and survival benefits. Group A is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal outdoor use at a price of $350?" Group B is asked: "Would you purchase this device for your organization at a price of $450, with a 10% discount for bulk orders?" Both groups are also asked about their current use of distress beacons and their awareness of the new FCC registration requirement.. Sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (Group A) and 100 emergency/outdoor organization representatives (Group B). Recruitment cost €2,000 (estimated).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (price sensitivity).. Predictions: T1: Group A purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$350; Group B purchase intent <30% because outdoor enthusiasts are the primary target.; T2: Group B purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$450; Group A purchase intent <30% because emergency services and organizations are the primary target.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥50% AND Group B purchase intent <30%, proceed with consumer-focused proposition (supports T1). If Group B purchase intent ≥50% AND Group A purchase intent <30%, proceed with B2B/government-focused proposition (supports T2). If both groups show ≥30% intent, both. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., the proposed consumer vs government demand survey) to validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., the proposed consumer vs government demand survey) to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (Group A) and emergency services/outdoor organizations (Group B) as identified in the test.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition would emphasize the 406 MHz distress beacon’s survival benefits and compliance advantage for outdoor users. A B2B/government proposition would emphasize the same benefits for search and rescue agencies,. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed consumer vs government demand survey (200 participants, €2,000 budget, 12 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for each group.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to limited evidence of actual consumer demand and market size. The survey will resolve this.. Would change if: If Group A purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$350, T1 becomes likely and the consumer proposition is justified.; If Group B purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$450, T2 becomes likely and the B2B/government proposition is justified.; If both groups show ≥30% intent, both theories remain uncertain and further testing is needed.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Musician vs Industrial Hearing Protection Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 200 participants: 100 self-identified musicians and 100 industrial workers. Randomly assign each participant to one of two conditions. Condition A: receive a description of a Hellberg musician hearing protector emphasizing sound-quality preservation and premium price. Condition B: receive a description of a Hellberg industrial hearing protector emphasizing compliance with safety regulations and integration into work processes, with a lower price point. Participants rate their. Sample: 200 participants (100 musicians, 100 industrial workers). Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale (1 = would not pay, 7 = would pay the highest price). 2) Choice (select either musician or industrial version).. Predictions: T1: Musicians in Condition A will report higher WTP and be more likely to choose the musician version than those in Condition B.; T2: Industrial workers in Condition B will report higher WTP and be more likely to choose the industrial version than those in Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for Condition A among musicians exceeds the average WTP for Condition B among industrial workers by at least €2 (a threshold reflecting a meaningful price difference) and the proportion choosing the musician version in Condition A is at least 15 percentage points. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.; Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.; Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.. Predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.; Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.. How value is captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.. Assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.; Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.; Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.; Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, multi‑purpose model (one compact tractor performing multiple tasks) and a status‑oriented model (same tractor styled with modern aesthetic, premium pricing). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary).. Sample: 500 U.S. households with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.. Measure: 1) WTP: maximum price participants would pay for each tractor concept. 2) Purchase intent: percentage indicating "Very likely" to buy each concept. 3) Secondary: perceived practicality (1‑10 scale) and perceived status (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Functional tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than status tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 10%.; T2: Status tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than functional tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 15%.. Decision rule: If functional tractor meets both WTP and purchase intent thresholds (e.g., purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ $2,500) and status tractor does not meet either threshold, proceed with a differentiated functional consumer proposition. If status tractor meets both thresholds and functional tractor does not, proceed with a differentiated status‑oriented consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds, . Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to empirically test whether a functional, multi‑purpose tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. If the survey confirms the functional model, proceed to develop a differentiated functional consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 200 participants: 100 musicians (recruited via music forums and schools) and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity groups and hiking forums). Each participant views a product description of a high-fidelity earplug (for musicians) or a lightweight, integrated earplug (for outdoor users). They are asked to indicate: (1) likelihood to purchase on a 1‑10 scale, (2) maximum price they would pay, (3) primary motivator (sound fidelity for musicians, comfort/weight for outdoor users).. Sample: 200 participants (100 musicians, 100 outdoor enthusiasts). Measure: Average purchase likelihood score for each segment; average maximum price willingness to pay for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Musicians will report higher purchase likelihood and willingness to pay for the high‑fidelity earplug than for the lightweight earplug.; T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will report higher purchase likelihood and willingness to pay for the lightweight earplug than for the high‑fidelity earplug.. Decision rule: If the average likelihood for musicians is at least 1.5 times higher than for outdoor enthusiasts AND the average willingness to pay for musicians is at least 1.5 times higher, then T1 is supported. If the average likelihood for outdoor enthusiasts is at least 1.5 times higher than for musicians AND the average willingness to pay for outdoor enthusiasts is at least 1.5 times higher, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase likelihood and willingness to pay for high-fidelity vs lightweight earplugs among musicians and outdoor enthusiasts. Until results are available, continue monitoring existing B2B/industrial sales and consider licensing Hellberg technology to third-party consumer brands as a low-risk alternative. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. Test "Expert Recommendation vs. Premium Perception Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 residential boat owners (DIY and leisure) in Scandinavia. Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a product description emphasizing Jotun’s premium marine coating features (durability, biofouling compliance, safety). Condition B receives the same description plus a simulated expert recommendation (e.g., "Recommended by marine experts for superior performance"). Both conditions see a price point 10% above Jotun’s. Sample: 300 residential boat owners (150 per condition) recruited via marine forums, DIY communities, and boat owner associations in Scandinavia.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP): maximum price participants would pay for Jotun marine coating. 2) Purchase intent: binary choice to "purchase Jotun marine coating" if offered at the stated price. 3) Self-reported importance of expert recommendation (1‑5 scale).. Predictions: T1: Condition A (premium description) will generate higher WTP and purchase intent than Condition B (same description + expert recommendation).; T2: Condition B (premium description + expert recommendation) will generate higher WTP and purchase intent than Condition A. If the difference between the two conditions is less than 5 percentage points, both theories are supported.. Decision rule: If Condition A’s average WTP exceeds Condition B’s by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium perception (T1 is more likely). If Condition B’s average WTP exceeds Condition A’s by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting expert‑driven. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue monitoring demand through sales data and consumer surveys before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, brand perception, or expert recommendations for Jotun marine coatings. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue monitoring demand through sales data and consumer surveys before committing resources. Target customer: Residential boat owners (DIY and leisure) in Scandinavia who purchase marine coatings.. Value proposition: A premium marine coating positioned as reliable, biofouling-compliant, and backed by Jotun’s existing distribution network, targeting consumers who value quality and safety.. T1: Musicians will adopt hearing protection if it does not impede listening and performing, because they value clear sound and performance ability over protection. Who benefits: Musicians and early-career musicians who need to hear clearly while protecting their hearing.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection does not reduce sound quality or affect performance, musicians are willing to use it consistently because it does not compromise their musical experience.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering models that preserve sound quality (e.g., active listening, FM radio) and by positioning its products as essential gear for musicians, justifying premium pricing.. Assumptions: Musicians are aware of hearing damage risks and prioritize clear sound over protection.; There is a market segment of musicians willing to pay for premium protection that does not hinder performance.; Hellberg can design products that meet these performance criteria.. Predictions: In a test offering a sound-preserving model to musicians, adoption rate will be higher than for standard protective earplugs.; Musicians will report satisfaction with sound quality and willingness to pay a premium price..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection if it is marketed as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, because they value style and status. Who benefits: Fashion-conscious consumers and early adopters who use accessories as a way to express identity.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is presented as a stylish, trendy product, consumers are motivated to purchase it as a status item rather than a functional necessity.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by creating fashionable designs, limited editions, and integrating brand storytelling, allowing premium pricing and repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with fashion and status.; There is a segment willing to pay a premium for stylish earplugs.; Hellberg can design products that meet aesthetic expectations without compromising protection.. Predictions: In a test offering a fashion-forward model, purchase intent will be higher than for standard protective earplugs.; Consumers will report that style is a primary purchase driver and will pay a premium for design..

T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, emergency-proven safety solution that can be used in remote, high-risk environments. Who benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need a device that can be used when other communication methods fail.. Why behaviour changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs in 2002 and the documented rescues (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts saved) create a perceived safety benefit; users trust a device that has proven its ability to summon help.. How value is captured: ACR can charge a premium price for a specialized outdoor PLB, sell through outdoor retailers and outdoor activity clubs, and potentially bundle with other safety gear.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety-proven outdoor gear.; Distribution channels (retailers, clubs) exist to reach this segment.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection does not reduce sound quality or affect performance, musicians are willing to use it consistently because it does not compromise their musical experience.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for models that preserve sound quality, and can differentiate its product line as the only hearing protection that musicians can reliably use during practice and performances.. Assumptions: Musicians are aware of hearing damage risks and prioritize clear sound over protection.; There is a market segment of musicians willing to pay a premium for functional hearing protection.; Hellberg can develop technology that preserves sound quality without compromising protection.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard and sound-preserving), musicians will choose the sound-preserving version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Surveyed willingness to pay will be higher for the sound-preserving model compared to standard earplugs..

T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt hearing protection if it is comfortable and discreet, because they value portability and integration with outdoor gear. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, cyclists) who need protection without compromising comfort or appearance.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is lightweight, breathable, and can be easily packed with other gear, users are more likely to carry and use it regularly during activities.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell premium outdoor-oriented earplugs at a higher price point, leveraging its existing reputation for comfort and safety.. Assumptions: Outdoor users prioritize weight and packability over protection.; There is a segment of outdoor enthusiasts willing to pay a premium for comfortable hearing protection.; Hellberg can design earplugs that meet outdoor performance standards without compromising safety.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard and outdoor-discreet), outdoor enthusiasts will choose the discreet version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Willingness to pay will be higher for the outdoor-discreet model compared to standard earplugs..

Test "Musician vs Outdoor Enthusiast Digital Ad Test" between T1; T2. Method: Run two parallel online ad campaigns targeting distinct audiences: musicians and outdoor enthusiasts. Each campaign will show a product image and a brief description emphasizing either performance-aid functionality (for musicians) or lightweight, discreet design (for outdoor enthusiasts). The ad will include a link to a landing page where visitors can register their intent to purchase (e.g., email address) and indicate their willingness to pay a price 20% above standard earplugs (musicians) or 15% above standard earplugs (outdoor).. Sample: Targeted to 1,000 musicians (via music forums, social media groups) and 1,000 outdoor enthusiasts (via outdoor activity forums, social media groups). Recruit via panel providers to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Conversion rate: percentage of visitors who register intent to purchase within 4 weeks. Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Musician conversion rate ≥ 15% and average WTP ≥ €120; Outdoor conversion rate < 10%.; T2: Outdoor conversion rate ≥ 15% and average WTP ≥ €100; Musician conversion rate < 10%.. Decision rule: If musician conversion ≥ 15% and average WTP ≥ €120, proceed with differentiated musician proposition. If outdoor conversion ≥ 15% and average WTP ≥ €100, proceed with differentiated outdoor proposition. If neither meets threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed digital ad test (X1) to empirically measure willingness to pay and conversion for a performance-aid musician proposition versus a lightweight outdoor proposition. Use the test results to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated musician proposition, a differentiated outdoor proposition, or no expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed digital ad test (X1) to empirically measure willingness to pay and conversion for a performance-aid musician proposition versus a lightweight outdoor proposition. Use the test results to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated musician proposition, a differentiated outdoor proposition, or no expansion. Target customer: Musicians and early‑career musicians who need reliable hearing protection without compromising performance.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protection product marketed as a performance aid that enhances listening experience, positioned as a premium, safety‑first accessory for musicians.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the digital ad test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €18,000 budget, measuring conversion and willingness to pay for the musician proposition.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for the respective propositions.. Would change if: If the test shows musician conversion ≥ 15% and average willingness to pay ≥ €120, the musician proposition becomes likely and further investment would be justified.; If the test shows outdoor conversion ≥ 15% and average willingness to pay ≥ €100, the outdoor proposition becomes likely and further investment would be justified.; If neither threshold is met, the recommendation would remain no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency backup for remote activities where other communication methods fail. Who benefits: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, paddlers) who travel in remote areas where mobile phones and radio signals are unavailable.. Why behaviour changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs for land-based emergencies and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts) create a perceived safety benefit that motivates purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can charge a premium price for a specialized consumer product, sell through outdoor retailers and emergency preparedness channels, and potentially bundle with other safety gear.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.; Consumers trust FCC approval as a safety endorsement.; Distribution channels exist to reach individual buyers.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate willingness to pay at least $300 for a 406 MHz PLB.; Sales in outdoor retail channels will increase after the FCC ruling.; Adoption rates will be higher in regions with high outdoor activity density..

T2: Emergency preparedness-focused consumers will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, low-cost emergency backup for home and travel safety, leveraging the FCC legalizing PLBs for land-based emergencies. Who benefits: Homeowners, travelers, and emergency preparedness enthusiasts who seek affordable emergency communication devices for remote or indoor use.. Why behaviour changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs for land use and the low cost of the device (e.g., $300) create a perceived cost-effective safety solution that motivates purchase, especially for those already interested in emergency preparedness.. How value is captured: ACR can sell through mass retail, online channels, and emergency preparedness retailers at a lower margin than premium outdoor segments, capturing volume sales and brand awareness among safety-conscious consumers.. Assumptions: Emergency preparedness market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.; Consumers view PLBs as a practical emergency backup, not just a luxury.; Distribution channels exist to reach broad consumer segments.. T1: Musicians will adopt hearing protection if it does not impede listening or performance, because they value clear sound and safety. Who benefits: Musicians and early‑career musicians who need to hear clearly while protecting their ears.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection does not reduce sound quality or affect performance, the barrier to adoption is removed, leading them to use it regularly.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering models that preserve sound quality, commanding premium prices and building brand loyalty among musicians.. Assumptions: Musicians are willing to pay more for hearing protection that does not compromise sound.; Clear sound is a primary purchase criterion for musicians.; Regular use of hearing protection is encouraged by performance needs.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of hearing protection (one with sound‑preserving technology and one without), the sound‑preserving version will achieve higher adoption rates among musicians.; Musicians will report higher satisfaction with sound quality when using the sound‑preserving version compared to standard earplugs..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection if it is marketed as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, because they value style and status. Who benefits: Fashion‑conscious consumers and early adopters who use accessories as self‑expression.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is presented as a trendy, stylish product, the primary purchase driver shifts from safety to personal expression, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by launching limited‑edition designs, collaborating with fashion brands, and commanding higher margins through premium positioning.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with style and status.; Fashion‑conscious buyers are willing to pay more for fashionable hearing protection.; Marketing can effectively reposition hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of hearing protection (one with fashion‑oriented design and one with standard design), the fashion version will achieve higher purchase intent among fashion‑conscious consumers.; Consumers will report higher perceived status when wearing the fashion version compared to standard earplugs..

Why behaviour changes: Creators seek to differentiate themselves from competitors and command higher rates; they are willing to pay more for gear that signals quality and expertise.. How value is captured: Neumann can charge premium prices for professional-grade products and sell through high-end distribution channels, capturing higher margins.. Randomly assign each creator to one of two scenarios: (A) premium professional microphone with status-focused marketing; (B) premium professional microphone with sound-quality focus. In each scenario, present a product description, price (e.g., €1,200), and a. Sample: 200 home-studio creators (100 tutorial creators, 100 paid content creators). Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) difference between scenarios. 2) Choice of scenario (status vs. sound quality). 3) Self-reported importance of status vs. sound quality.. Predictions: T1: Creators will show higher WTP and choose the status-focused scenario, indicating prestige drives purchase.; T2: Creators will show higher WTP and choose the sound-quality focused scenario, indicating performance drives purchase.. Decision rule: If the difference in average WTP between scenarios exceeds 15% (e.g., status scenario WTP is at least 15% higher than sound-quality scenario), proceed with differentiated offering (status-focused). T1: Home-studio creators will adopt premium microphones if they perceive the product as a status symbol and a signal of professional credibility, leading them to purchase despite higher prices. Who benefits: Creators seeking to elevate their brand and signal expertise; Neumann benefits by commanding premium prices and building a premium brand image.. Why behaviour changes: Creators use equipment as a visible indicator of skill and quality; a product associated with professionals and high-end audio reinforces that signal.. How value is captured: Neumann can price microphones at premium levels and sell through distribution channels that emphasize brand prestige, capturing higher margins.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to allocate budget to equipment as a branding asset.; Professional association influences purchase decisions beyond functional need.; Premium pricing is acceptable if perceived as part of a prestige ecosystem.. Predictions: Creators will express willingness to pay at least 20% above standard professional prices for a product marketed as premium.; Purchase intent will be higher when presented with creator testimonials emphasizing professional status.; Sales of premium-branded microphones will correlate with creator influence metrics (e.g., social media following, online views)..

T2: Home-studio creators will adopt premium microphones primarily because they need higher sound quality for professional-grade production, and are willing to pay more for performance that meets that standard. Who benefits: Creators seeking studio-quality audio; Neumann benefits by selling premium products at higher margins, leveraging its professional reputation for audio excellence.. Why behaviour changes: Creators prioritize audio fidelity as a critical component of high-quality content; they are willing to invest in equipment that demonstrably improves output quality.. How value is captured: Neumann can price microphones based on technical performance claims and market them as essential tools for professional-level results, capturing higher margins and premium positioning.. Assumptions: Creators evaluate microphones primarily on sound quality, not brand prestige.; Professional-grade audio is a core requirement for creator workflows.; Higher price reflects superior performance, not status.. Predictions: Creators will express willingness to pay at least 15% above standard professional prices for a product marketed on sound-quality performance.; Purchase intent will be higher when presented with technical specifications and audio comparisons.; Sales of premium-branded microphones will correlate with creator production metrics (e.g., project complexity, critical listening sessions)..

case.question: Should Hellberg Safety develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Hellberg Safety should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must consider current reach to individual buyers (unknown from brief).; Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, outdoor enthusiasts).; 2) Expand the existing hearing‑protection line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., fashion‑oriented earplugs, premium branding).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B/industrial customers and current consumer offering without new consumer propositions.; 4) License Hellberg technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer proposition..

T1: Consumers in target use cases will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product when it is marketed as a safety-first solution that meets functional requirements (e.g., certified protection, comfort, compatibility with activities) and is positioned as a reliable brand, because they prioritize safety and are willing to pay a premium for proven effectiveness. Who benefits: Consumers seeking safe hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, outdoor enthusiasts).. Why behaviour changes: When a product is promoted as meeting stringent safety standards and is associated with a reputable brand, users feel confidence in its performance, reducing perceived risk and encouraging purchase despite price.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for safety-certified products and build brand trust, capturing value through higher margins and brand loyalty.. Assumptions: Consumers in target segments are aware of safety certification and value it.; Brand reputation from existing industrial B2B work transfers to consumer perception of safety.; Willingness to pay a premium for certified safety is sufficient to cover any cost increase.. Predictions: In a test market, a safety‑focused proposition will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay compared to a generic, non‑safety proposition for the same product.; Surveyed consumers will report safety as the primary reason for choosing the safety‑focused product over alternatives..

T2: Consumers in target use cases will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product when it is marketed as a fashion or lifestyle accessory that aligns with personal style and social signaling, because they seek products that reflect their identity and are willing to pay for aesthetics and status. Who benefits: Consumers who use hearing protection as a visible accessory and status symbol, especially younger demographics and early adopters.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is presented as a stylish, trendy item rather than a safety device, users associate it with personal expression and social acceptance, increasing purchase motivation beyond functional need.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price products at premium levels, sell through lifestyle channels, and build a brand that is aspirational, capturing value through higher margins and brand equity.. Assumptions: Consumers in target segments value personal expression and are willing to pay for style.; Fashion trends influence hearing-protection choices more than safety certification alone.; Brand positioning as a lifestyle product can overcome perceived safety concerns.. Predictions: In a test market, a fashion‑focused proposition will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay compared to a safety‑focused proposition for the same product.; Surveyed consumers will cite style or status as the primary reason for choosing the fashion product over safety‑focused alternatives..

Test "Safety vs Fashion Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a safety‑focused proposition (emphasizing certified protection, comfort, compatibility) or a fashion‑focused proposition (emphasizing style, status, personal expression). Participants are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay (WTP) for the exposed product.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–45 who have attended live music events (e.g., concerts, festivals) in the past year, and who report using hearing protection at least occasionally. Recruitment via an online panel to match demographic distribution.. Measure: Primary outcome: average WTP (EUR) for the exposed product. Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and stated primary motivation (safety vs style).. Predictions: T1: Safety‑focused proposition will yield higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than the fashion proposition.; T2: Fashion‑focused proposition will yield higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than the safety proposition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the safety proposition exceeds the average WTP for the fashion proposition by at least €10 (or a 10‑point difference on a 10‑point scale), proceed with a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the fashion proposition exceeds the safety proposition by at least €10, proceed with a fashion‑focused proposition. If the. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Safety vs Fashion Proposition Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for safety-focused versus fashion-focused hearing protection among target consumers. The test will determine whether a safety-first proposition drives higher demand, which would justify investment in a differentiated consumer proposition. Until results are available, continue monitoring existing B2B/ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-C shows that styled protectors increase wear frequency, which aligns with the premise that appearance and style can drive adoption. It does not contradict T1, which focuses on safety-first messaging, but rather complements it by showing that aesthetic appeal can increase usage even when safety is not the primary frame. New claim: Consumers in target use cases will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product when it is marketed as a safety-first solution that meets functional requirements (e.g., certified protection, comfort, compatibility) AND is styled to be visually appealing, because both safety and appearance motivate purchase.. Evidence: SYN-C.
